Pristine 1967 Dodge Coronet R/T Has a Rare Feature in Plain Sight
18 photos
Photo: basilclassiccars.com
The Dodge Coronet was first introduced in 1949 as a full-size car , but it's mainly iconic for the years it spent in the intermediate market. Discontinued in 1959, the Coronet returned in 1965 as a mid-size car. It was part of the muscle car wars and used as a base for two of Dodge's most iconic models, the Charger and Super Bee.
The Coronet is obviously overshadowed by the other two Mopars. But that's not to say that the Coronet is not a proper muscle car with the right features. Sure, most of the vehicles sold were mundane sedans and station wagons, but the two-door models were available with Chrysler's hottest golden-era mill, the 426-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) Hemi V8.
And here's a fact that many of us tend to forget: the Coronet was the very first Dodge to feature the R/T badge. We often associate the emblem with the Charger, which got it in 1968, but the Coronet R/T arrived a year earlier. It was only available as a two-door hardtop and convertible and came standard with the 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) RB, available only with a four-barrel carburetor at the time.
The Hemi was on the R/T's options list, while transmission choices included the three-speed TorqueFlite automatic and the four-speed manual. 1970 was the final year for the Coronet R/T. In 1971, Dodge redesigned the Coronet as a four-door model only, with the Super Bee version moved on the Charger platform.
As Dodge's bread-and-butter intermediate, the Coronet was quite popular overall. However, only a small fraction of these cars were ordered in R/T specs. Specifically, Dodge sold over 700,000 units between 1967 and 1970, but only 30,896 examples were R/T cars. That's less than 5% of the total output.
Two thirds of these R/Ts were sold in the first two model years. The numbers split almost evenly, with 10,181 delivered in 1967. The blue example you see here is one of those cars, but it's not as common as the production number suggests. This Mopar has a rare factory feature in plain sight; I'm talking about the convertible top.
You see, while most mid-size cars were available in this body style at the time, drop tops were far from popular. This feature alone puts the Coronet R/T into three-digit territory, as Dodge sold only 628 cars. And needless to say, the blue-on-blue color combo makes it even rarer (the soft top is white, so no triple-blue treatment here).
The Mopar packs the 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) RB rated at 375 horsepower, which was the standard mill. It mates with a three-speed TorqueFlite automatic. It's unclear how many were ordered with this transmission, but we're probably looking at under 400 examples.
Rarity aside, this Coronet R/T is a gem. The car has been restored and looks flawless inside and out, while the engine bay is equally clean. And it's also notably more affordable than a Hemi. Currently parked in the Basil Classic Cars showroom in Depew, New York, the Coronet R/T has a $49,388 sticker. Check it out in the video below.
